verses.1: Al-Mizan treats the verse as an oath by night as it veils the day; the thing covered may be the earth or the sun.
verses.2: Al-Mizan defines tajallā as the appearance of what had been hidden. It notes the contrast between the present tense for night covering and the past tense for the day's appearance.
verses.3: Al-Mizan reads mā as the Almighty God, with the use of what rather than who lending an ambiguity that magnifies Him and His creation of male and female polarities. It rejects treating mā as a verbal-noun particle and takes male and female without restriction, rather than as humans alone or Adam and Eve.
verses.4: Al-Mizan defines saʿy here as deliberately pursued action, though its root denotes walking quickly, and la-shattā as diverse. The oath's conclusion is that human endeavors differ in themselves and consequences: some involve giving, God-consciousness, and affirmation of good, while others involve miserliness, avarice, and denial, each with its own result.
verses.5: Al-Mizan says that giving, opposed here to miserliness, means spending wealth in God's way, and that wariness explains it as religiously committed spending. Bil-ḥusnā affirms the promised good reward, which entails belief in resurrection, God's sole lordship and divinity, and the messengers through whom that reward is promised.

verses.7: Al-Mizan defines taysīr as preparation or arrangement and yusrā as ease without hardship. It may mean divine grace that makes righteous action easy, or preparation for eternal happiness and abiding in paradise; the latter better accords with the Qur'an's promises.
verses.8: Al-Mizan glosses bukhl as the opposite of iʿṭāʾ, giving or spending, and istighnāʾ as seeking wealth by retaining and hoarding it. Denying al-ḥusnā is denying the good promise and divine reward conveyed by prophets and messengers, and thereby entails denial of resurrection.
verses.9: Al-Mizan glosses bukhl as the opposite of iʿṭāʾ, giving or spending, and istighnāʾ as seeking wealth by retaining and hoarding it. Denying al-ḥusnā is denying the good promise and divine reward conveyed by prophets and messengers, and thereby entails denial of resurrection.
verses.10: Al-Mizan takes being eased into hardship as being left without divine support: good deeds become burdensome and the breast does not open to faith. Alternatively, it means being prepared for divine punishment.
verses.11: Al-Mizan glosses taraddī as falling from a height and applies it to descent into the grave, collapse into hellfire, or destruction. Mā may ask what wealth could help at death and perdition, or deny that any wealth can help.
verses.12: Al-Mizan explains that God's easing of one group toward ease and another toward hardship belongs to the guidance He has undertaken by wisdom, whether the verse explains that custom or the present instruction. Guidance first means showing the path of servitude, an act properly God's even though prophets guide by His leave; people may nevertheless follow or refuse it. It also means bringing a person to the intended perfection—a wholesome life or felicitous afterlife—which belongs to God as creational guidance, though He may act through subordinate intermediaries. The verse can bear either sense, and its unqualified wording most naturally includes both legislative direction and real guidance to the destination. Easing the righteous and the wicked to their differing outcomes is interdependent: like the Qur'an itself, one divine guidance becomes mercy for believers and increase of loss for wrongdoers.
verses.13: Al-Mizan reads the afterlife and prior as the realms of return and instantiation. Every thing exists only as upheld by al-Qayyūm, so God alone truly owns all things; every conventional ownership and power of control rests on His grant. Nothing can impede His ownership, judgment, or will.
verses.14: Al-Mizan takes the opening fa as drawing the warning of hell from God's undertaking to guide. The shift from the preceding first-person plural to singular marks God as the true and primary Warner, who delivers the warning through His Messenger. Talaẓẓā denotes the flaming and flaring of the fire of hell.
verses.15: Al-Mizan identifies the most wretched as disbelievers who deny the true call and turn away, using the comparison rather than a claim about one uniquely wretched person. Their otherworldly misery is worse than worldly suffering because it is eternal, whereas worldly affliction can end. Ṣaly is perpetual attachment to the fire and thus eternal burning. Against the view that the verse excludes corrupt believers from hell altogether, the commentary says it confines eternal torment to such disbelievers while allowing that others may enter hell temporarily.

verses.17: Al-Mizan says tajannub is being kept far from the fire. The wariest are not one superlative individual over all people, but those whose Godwariness manifests in giving their wealth for purification, unlike those cautious only about worldly loss or otherwise pious without this giving. The description is general, even if a revelation circumstance is reported, because such a circumstance does not restrict its application; the singular-superlative reading would also make the universal warning incoherent. These givers do not repay anyone's favor: they seek only the face of their Lord, the Most Sublime. They will be pleased with the highest and most precious recompense, fitting His lordship and sublimity.
